name: Pencil Hatching
basis: why: tone from layers of parallel strokes; how: up to four hatch layers by darkness thresholds, hand wobble, paper tooth
note: Hatching is shared with pen and engraving; filed by the medium named.

lumenary.blurb: Tone built the way an illustrator does it: parallel strokes first, then a second set across them, darker passes where the shadows are deepest.

facts.bestOn: Objects and portraits with strong form

why: An illustrator builds tone from layers of parallel strokes: one set in one direction, a second across it, more where the shadow is deepest. A light area has none, a mid tone has one set and the deepest shadow is crossed four times. This treatment stacks up to four layers at different angles, each appearing only once the picture is dark enough.
how: Set up to four layers of strokes at 45, 135, 0 and 90 degrees, all turned together by the turn slider.
Let a layer appear only when the darkness passes its threshold of 0.16, 0.34, 0.54 or 0.74.
For each layer, divide the position across the strokes by the line spacing, with slow noise for the hand’s wobble, and take the integer part as the stroke index.
Make each stroke thicker the further the darkness is past the threshold, with its own random width and pressure seeded by its index.
Combine layers by taking the strongest, lighten with paper tooth, and add optional soft outlines.
history: Hatching and cross-hatching were developed in drawing and engraving long before photography, by artists such as Albrecht Dürer, who used them to model form in prints. Graphite was found at Borrowdale in England in the 1560s, and the modern pencil followed. Today hatching is used in comics, manga, technical illustration and architectural sketches.
terms: Parallel lines used to suggest shade.
A second set of lines crossing the first to make a darker tone.
The grain of paper that catches the pencil.
paragraphs: An illustrator builds tone from layers of parallel strokes: one set in one direction, a second set across it, a third and a fourth where the shadow is deepest. The program does the same with up to four layers whose strokes run at 45, 135, 0 and 90 degrees (all turned together by the turn slider). A layer begins to appear only when the picture’s darkness d passes its threshold t, which is 0.16, 0.34, 0.54 and 0.74 (stretched by 1.3 when there are only two layers), so highlights stay paper and the deepest shadows are crossed four times.

For one layer, the position across the strokes is the pixel’s coordinate along the layer’s normal divided by the line spacing, with slow noise added so the hand wobbles. The integer part of that number is the index of the stroke, the fractional part says where in the stroke the pixel lies. The stroke is thicker the further the darkness is past the threshold, each stroke has its own random width and pressure (seeded by its index, so every pixel along it agrees), and the layers combine by taking the strongest. Paper tooth lightens the whole thing by up to 30%, and optional soft outlines add a faint contour.

equations.note: s is the line spacing, ω the hand wobble, ν slow noise; ⌊u⌋ is the stroke number and f the place inside it.
Stroke width grows with how far the darkness d is past the layer’s threshold.
Ink coverage at the pixel; π_k is the random pressure (0.62 to 1) of its stroke in layer k.

presets.text: Two layers with a bold turn is a quick, graphic sketch.
Red lead on cream paper feels like an old study.
Tighter spacing and full layers give a smooth, almost photographic result.
